name: Usable Security & Privacy
description: Human factors: user studies, mental models, warnings, and the usability of security and privacy tools.

uss.narrative:
Usable security and privacy research in this period began by zeroing in on the everyday tools and policies that mediate user decisions. The earliest listed work attacked the comprehension problem head-on: "Polisis: Automated Analysis and Presentation of Privacy Policies Using Deep Learning" (USENIX 2018) used machine learning to make impenetrable privacy policies queryable, while several password studies that same year -- "Better managed than memorized? Studying the Impact of Managers on Password Strength and Reuse" and "Forgetting of Passwords: Ecological Theory and Data" -- probed why authentication keeps failing users. At the same time, the field began stretching past the single user: "Rethinking Access Control and Authentication for the Home Internet of Things (IoT)" (USENIX 2018) argued that multi-user devices break the assumptions baked into traditional access control.

The major shift across 2019-2020 was a turn toward vulnerable and at-risk populations and the social context of security. "Clinical Computer Security for Victims of Intimate Partner Violence" (USENIX 2019) reframed security as something delivered through human-centered, clinical interventions, and was reinforced by work on human trafficking survivors and, in 2020, "The Tools and Tactics Used in Intimate Partner Surveillance" -- collectively establishing interpersonal abuse as a core research agenda. In parallel, the multi-user theme matured with "Understanding and Improving Security and Privacy in Multi-User Smart Homes" (USENIX 2019) and branched into emerging platforms via "Secure Multi-User Content Sharing for Augmented Reality Applications" (USENIX 2019). A second strand recognized that developers are users too: "Stack Overflow Considered Helpful! Deep Learning Security Nudges Towards Stronger Cryptography" (2019) and "Understanding security mistakes developers make" (2020) treated developer behavior as a usability problem in its own right.

By 2020-2021 the work scaled up and got more empirical, measuring real systems and large populations: "A Comprehensive Quality Evaluation of Security and Privacy Advice on the Web" (2020) audited the advice ecosystem, while "Empirical Measurement of Systemic 2FA Usability" (2020) and "Driving 2FA Adoption at Scale" (2021) moved authentication research from lab studies to deployment-scale optimization. Global and collective perspectives also emerged, from "A Large Scale Study of User Behavior, Expectations and Engagement with Android Permissions" (2021) to "Collective Information Security in Large-Scale Urban Protests: the Case of Hong Kong" (2021).

Most recently the area has confronted harder conceptual and methodological questions and new threat surfaces. "What Are the Chances? Explaining the Epsilon Parameter in Differential Privacy" (USENIX 2023) tackled the usability of an abstract mathematical privacy notion, and "Ethical Frameworks and Computer Security Trolley Problems" (2023) pushed the community to formalize how it reasons about research ethics. The at-risk and emerging-platform threads converged in "Abuse Vectors: A Framework for Conceptualizing IoT-Enabled Interpersonal Abuse" (2023) and "Exploring User Reactions and Mental Models Towards Perceptual Manipulation Attacks in Mixed Reality" (2023), showing the field now studies mental models against AI- and immersive-tech-driven threats like those in "DeepPhish" (2022). The trajectory runs from making existing tools and policies understandable, to centering vulnerable users and developers, to rigorous large-scale measurement, and finally to grappling with the usability and ethics of frontier privacy techniques and immersive systems.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this NDSS thread grew out of a simple worry: the security and privacy machinery users interact with every day is often opaque or misleading. "Investigating Ad Transparency Mechanisms in Social Media" (NDSS 2018) checked whether Facebook's "why am I seeing this ad?" explanations actually reflected how targeting worked, while "Didn't You Hear Me? - Towards More Successful Web Vulnerability Notifications" (NDSS 2018) asked why the people who most need a security warning so often ignore it. Both framed the field's core tension between what a system tells users and what users understand. "The Crux of Voice (In)Security" (NDSS 2019) sharpened this by literally studying users' brains as they tried, and failed, to detect impersonated voices.

Around 2020 the area split into two energetic tracks. One reimagined authentication for new hardware and channels: "OcuLock" (NDSS 2020) and later "SoundLock" (NDSS 2023) turned VR headsets' eye and pupil signals into login biometrics. The other measured how ordinary people react to real-world security signals, from "Are You Going to Answer That?" on anti-robocall indicators (NDSS 2020) to "A View from the Cockpit" on pilots facing avionics attacks (NDSS 2020). A parallel compliance-and-policy line matured alongside, running from "Compliance Cautions" (NDSS 2020) and "Above and Beyond" (NDSS 2022) through automated privacy-policy tooling like "PrivacyFlash Pro" (NDSS 2021). The 2021 audit "Hey Alexa, is this Skill Safe?" became a heavily-cited landmark for exposing how a whole voice-assistant ecosystem obscured who users were really trusting.

By 2023–2024 the work grew more rigorous and, notably, larger in scale. "Folk Models of Misinformation on Social Media" (NDSS 2023) and "A Systematic Study of the Consistency of Two-Factor Authentication User Journeys" (NDSS 2023) formalized the mental-models and consistency questions, while "Don't Interrupt Me" (NDSS 2024) took warning-fatigue research to production scale by studying permission-prompt quieting inside real Chrome. Policy comprehension also went computational, with "Towards Automated Regulation Analysis" (NDSS 2024) and "PolicyPulse" (NDSS 2025) using NLP to make dense privacy text legible.

The most recent papers show the field broadening to new populations, new roles, and new interaction surfaces. NDSS 2025 studied who exactly is vulnerable — teens and adults facing "YouTube Giveaway Scams," corporate boards making cyber-risk decisions, and how the precise wording of rationales sways choices in "The Power of Words." Developers and configurators became first-class subjects too, in "Attributing Open-Source Contributions is Critical but Difficult" and "Translating C To Rust: Lessons from a User Study." That momentum carries straight into 2026, where "Mapping the Cloud" and "Action Required" tackle the human side of cloud and CI/CD misconfiguration, "From Perception to Protection" centers XR developers, and "Anchors of Trust" (NDSS 2026) studies awareness, consent, and control as authentication now stretches across multiple linked devices — the newest frontier for a field that began by simply asking whether users understood what their tools were telling them.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection treats usable security as fundamentally about people in specific, often vulnerable situations rather than an abstract "average user." IEEE S&P 2018 opened with a cluster of studies on populations that mainstream security tools ignore: "The Spyware Used in Intimate Partner Violence" (S&P 2018) documented how abusers weaponize consumer apps against survivors, "Computer Security and Privacy for Refugees in the United States" (S&P 2018) and "On Enforcing the Digital Immunity of a Large Humanitarian Organization" (S&P 2018) extended the lens to displaced and crisis-affected people, while "Hackers vs. Testers: A Comparison of Software Vulnerability Discovery Processes" (S&P 2018) turned the human-factors lens on security professionals themselves. Alongside these sat early usability evaluations of concrete mechanisms, notably "A Tale of Two Studies: The Best and Worst of YubiKey Usability" (S&P 2018).

Around 2019-2020 the field matured methodologically and broadened its targets. "How Well Do My Results Generalize? Comparing Security and Privacy Survey Results from MTurk, Web, and Telephone Samples" (S&P 2019) forced the community to reckon with whether its crowdsourced findings held up, becoming a touchstone for study design. Mental-models research crystallized with "'If HTTPS Were Secure, I Wouldn't Need 2FA' - End User and Administrator Mental Models of HTTPS" (S&P 2019), and authentication usability advanced through "Is FIDO2 the Kingslayer of User Authentication? A Comparative Usability Study of FIDO2 Passwordless Authentication" (S&P 2020) and "This PIN Can Be Easily Guessed: Analyzing the Security of Smartphone Unlock PINs" (S&P 2020). A parallel thread pushed transparency as a usability intervention: "Ask the Experts: What Should Be on an IoT Privacy and Security Label?" (S&P 2020) and "Security Update Labels: Establishing Economic Incentives for Security Patching of IoT Consumer Products" (S&P 2020) argued that nutrition-style labels could make invisible security properties legible to buyers, while "Towards Effective Differential Privacy Communication for Users' Data Sharing Decision and Comprehension" (S&P 2020) grappled with explaining formal privacy to lay users.

The early 2020s consolidated these threads into named research agendas and moved upstream to the developers and organizations that build tools. "SoK: Hate, Harassment, and the Changing Landscape of Online Abuse" (S&P 2021) and especially "SoK: A Framework for Unifying At-Risk User Research" (S&P 2022) gave the scattered vulnerable-population studies a shared vocabulary, later complemented by the ethics-and-methods guidance of "SoK: Safer Digital-Safety Research Involving At-Risk Users" (S&P 2024). At the same time the community accepted that usability failures often originate before software ships, studying practitioners in "How Does Usable Security (Not) End Up in Software Products? Results From a Qualitative Interview Study" (S&P 2022), "Committed to Trust: A Qualitative Study on Security & Trust in Open Source Software Projects" (S&P 2022), and "'They're not that hard to mitigate': What Cryptographic Library Developers Think About Timing Attacks" (S&P 2022), while "Phishing in Organizations: Findings from a Large-Scale and Long-Term Study" (S&P 2022) tested defenses at real-world scale.

The most recent work (S&P 2024-2026) is defined by two forces: generative AI and a globalizing, regulation-shaped view of who needs protection. "A Representative Study on Human Detection of Artificially Generated Media Across Countries" (S&P 2024) measured how poorly people spot forgeries, and the 2026 cohort turns LLMs into both subject and threat, from "Can Foundation LLMs Accurately Estimate Password Strength and Provide Appropriate Password Feedback?" and "Investigating the Impact of Dark Patterns on LLM-Based Web Agents" to smarter warning design in "From 'Be Careful' to 'Here's Why': Investigating User Reasoning with Context-Specific SMS Scam Warnings" (S&P 2026). Authentication usability continues its long arc with "The Passkey Promise: A Comparative Usability Study of MFA Methods" (S&P 2026), while the field's center of gravity shifts toward specific populations and legal contexts in "Perceived Privacy Risk and Mitigation Post-Roe" (S&P 2026), "Papers, Please: A First Look at Age Verification on the Web" (S&P 2026), "Privacy Perspectives and Practices of Chinese Smart Home Product Teams" (S&P 2026), and "'I Wonder if These Warnings are Accurate': Security and Privacy Advice in Nine Majority World Countries" (S&P 2026) — a clear signal that usable security now sees its users as globally diverse and its threats as increasingly AI-mediated.

ccs.narrative:
Usable security research at CCS examines the human dimension of security systems, from password policies to AI assistant risks. The 2018-2019 cohort mixed measurement and design: On the Accuracy of Password Strength Meters (CCS 2018) revealed that widely deployed meters poorly predict real password strength, and Investigating System Operators' Perspective on Security Misconfigurations (CCS 2018) explained why configuration errors persist despite tool availability. (Un)informed Consent: Studying GDPR Consent Notices in the Field (CCS 2019) became one of the most-cited CCS papers by documenting how consent interfaces mislead users at scale.

The 2019-2020 period deepened professional security contexts. Matched and Mismatched SOCs: A Qualitative Study on Security Operations Center Issues (CCS 2019) identified the organizational factors that undermine SOC effectiveness, and A Qualitative Study of Dependency Management and Its Security Implications (CCS 2020) exposed the developer behaviors that perpetuate vulnerable dependency chains.

AI-assisted development became a major usable security concern in 2023: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants? (CCS 2023) demonstrated that developers with Copilot-style tools produce more insecure code while paradoxically feeling more confident about its security. This paper connected usable security with the newly prominent AI security agenda, setting a direction the community was still pursuing through 2024-2025.

milestones.title: On the Accuracy of Password Strength Meters
milestones.note: Showed that widely deployed password strength meters systematically misestimate real password strength.

milestones.title: Investigating System Operators' Perspective on Security Misconfigurations
milestones.note: Revealed the human and organizational factors behind persistent security misconfigurations in production systems.

milestones.title: (Un)informed Consent: Studying GDPR Consent Notices in the Field
milestones.note: The definitive study of GDPR consent dark patterns showing most notices are manipulative rather than informative.

milestones.title: Matched and Mismatched SOCs: A Qualitative Study on Security Operations Center Issues
milestones.note: Uncovered organizational mismatches and human factors that degrade security analyst effectiveness in SOCs.

milestones.title: A Qualitative Study of Dependency Management and Its Security Implications
milestones.note: Explained developer decision-making around dependency updates and why vulnerable libraries persist in codebases.

milestones.title: "I need a better description": An Investigation Into User Expectations For Differential Privacy
milestones.note: Showed users have miscalibrated expectations of DP, informing how technical privacy guarantees should be communicated.

milestones.title: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?
milestones.note: Demonstrated AI coding assistants increase insecure code production while giving developers false security confidence.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this slice reads like a field mapping out where human effort and security collide. Some studies focused on making opaque systems legible: "Polisis: Automated Analysis and Presentation of Privacy Policies Using Deep Learning" (USENIX 2018) tried to translate unreadable privacy policies into something users could act on, while "On the Accuracy of Password Strength Meters" (CCS 2018) and "A Tale of Two Studies: The Best and Worst of YubiKey Usability" (S&P 2018) scrutinized the everyday tools — meters, 2FA keys — that are supposed to help people be secure but often confuse them. At the same time, a striking thread turned attention to people the field had ignored: "The Spyware Used in Intimate Partner Violence" (S&P 2018) and "Computer Security and Privacy for Refugees in the United States" (S&P 2018) showed that threat models look very different for vulnerable populations, and that usability failures can be a matter of safety.

By 2019-2020 the area matured along three axes. First, methods became self-reflective — "How Well Do My Results Generalize? Comparing Security and Privacy Survey Results from MTurk, Web, and Telephone Samples" (S&P 2019) forced the community to question its own crowdsourced data, and regulation-driven work like "(Un)informed Consent: Studying GDPR Consent Notices in the Field" (CCS 2019) measured how real deployments of consent notices actually behaved. Second, the at-risk thread hardened into a research program, moving from documentation to intervention with "Clinical Computer Security for Victims of Intimate Partner Violence" (USENIX 2019). Third, the field followed technology into new domains: multi-user smart homes ("Understanding and Improving Security and Privacy in Multi-User Smart Homes," USENIX 2019), IoT transparency labels ("Ask the Experts: What Should Be on an IoT Privacy and Security Label?," S&P 2020), and passwordless login ("Is FIDO2 the Kingslayer of User Authentication?," S&P 2020). A parallel shift widened the "user" beyond consumers to developers and operators, as in "Understanding security mistakes developers make" (USENIX 2020) and "Investigating System Operators' Perspective on Security Misconfigurations" (CCS 2018).

The early 2020s consolidated these strands into frameworks and confronted emerging technologies head-on. "SoK: Hate, Harassment, and the Changing Landscape of Online Abuse" (S&P 2021) and "SoK: A Framework for Unifying At-Risk User Research" (S&P 2022) gave the vulnerable-user literature shared vocabulary, while AR/VR usability crystallized in "SoK: Authentication in Augmented and Virtual Reality" (S&P 2022), building on earlier probes like "OcuLock" (NDSS 2020). Abstract concepts got usability scrutiny too, with "'I need a better description': An Investigation Into User Expectations For Differential Privacy" (CCS 2021). The clearest inflection point, though, is AI: "Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?" (CCS 2023) opened the question of how human-AI collaboration reshapes security outcomes.

The most recent work, clustered in NDSS 2026 and S&P 2026, shows the area splitting its attention between refining old problems and chasing AI-native ones. Classic usability questions persist in sharper form — cross-device login in "Anchors of Trust" (NDSS 2026), password-manager UI attacks in "Vault Raider" (NDSS 2026), and warning design in "From 'Be Careful' to 'Here's Why': Investigating User Reasoning with Context-Specific SMS Scam Warnings" (S&P 2026), which pushes past generic alerts toward explanations users can reason about. The developer- and operator-centered thread continues in "Mapping the Cloud" and "Action Required: A Mixed-Methods Study of Security Practices in GitHub Actions" (both NDSS 2026), and the XR line matures into "From Perception to Protection: A Developer-Centered Study of Security and Privacy Threats in Extended Reality" (NDSS 2026). Meanwhile the newest frontier reframes usability around autonomous agents rather than people, as "Investigating the Impact of Dark Patterns on LLM-Based Web Agents" (S&P 2026) asks what manipulation and safety even mean when the "user" clicking through the web is itself an AI.
